method: Each homepage was read with WebFetch, which returns a text/markup summary. Visual attributes (typeface, scale, colour, sticky headers, true mobile layout) are mostly NOT observable through it and are recorded as not determinable rather than guessed. Rules marked 'derived' are not observed on any site read and are principles of honest design for Kora's generator.

rules.rule: Open with the work itself (a featured-project showcase or a one-line positioning statement followed immediately by a link to all work), not with an about-us paragraph.
Keep primary navigation to 4-6 top-level items built around Work, About, Contact (plus Services/News only if real content exists); put depth in dropdowns or filters.
Let imagery be the studio's own project work (photography, renders, screens), shown large with a title and one line; avoid generic stock photography.
Make the work index filterable by discipline or service (tabs or filter lists) so one page serves several visitor intents.
Keep copy sparse and image-led; sections are short headings plus a link, not paragraphs.
Use named clients/projects as the trust cue, placed high on the page (client roster or featured project), and add awards only if the owner has actually won them.
Provide a persistent contact route in the nav and again near the footer, phrased as starting a project or getting in touch; a newsletter is an optional secondary path.
Include a News/Latest or editorial layer in the architecture (a few cards linking to articles or press) to show the studio is active.

If the owner has no clients, awards or case studies yet: show a small number of clearly labelled self-initiated or concept projects, the founders' names and photos, and the studio's process; never invent client logos or awards. (derived, not observed)

Typography and mobile behaviour were not observable by text fetch; for the generator, default to one confident sans display face with large headings and restrained body text, and a collapsed menu on mobile. (derived, unverified)

Read 2026-11-07. Server-rendered. Nav (6): Services, Industries, Case Studies, Resources, Blog, Let's Talk. Hero headline about experience when stakes are high, single 'Let's talk' CTA, team-headshot grid. Then featured case study (client logo, tags, summary, testimonial), stage-based services links, wall of 24 monochrome client logos under a '1,000+ outcomes' heading, product promos, AI service highlight with line illustration, three case-study cards, 'purpose-driven teams' blurb, six resource cards, closing CTA, footer with US and UK phone numbers. rules.rule: Headline states the outcome the client gets (e.g. products people keep using, reliability under pressure) rather than the company name or a list of technologies.
Use 5-6 top-level nav items covering Services, Work/Case studies, Insights/Blog, About and a visible Contact/Let's talk item.
Funnel every call-to-action to a single contact/hire path with consistent wording ('Let's talk', 'Contact us'), repeated in header, mid-page and closing section.
Sequence trust cues as: client names/logos, one or two measurable facts, a named testimonial, then case studies; every figure must be owner-supplied and dated.
Present case studies as cards with client, short outcome summary and a read-more link, with one featured above the fold of the second screen.
Summarise capabilities in 3-4 short named blocks or stage-based links, not long service lists.
Favour abstract graphics, diagrams and line illustration (plus team headshots) over stock photos of people at laptops.
Include a resources/insights section (articles, guides, podcast, newsletter) as secondary content under the main funnel.
Show security/quality credentials (ISO, B Corp etc.) in the footer only when the owner holds them.

With no clients or case studies yet, show the team, the working method (discovery, build, handover), open-source or own-product work and written insights as honest proof; do not fabricate logos, scores or testimonials. (derived)

rules.rule: Let the photographs be the hero: open on a full-bleed image or image grid with little or no headline copy.
Keep the nav small (3-7 items) and organise the work by genre or theme (People/Places/Things, Portraits/Lifestyle) rather than by date.
Minimise text: labels and short captions only, so type never competes with the images.
Keep density very low: few sections, one gallery or a short curated set, generous spacing.
Give enquiries a simple, obvious path (email link or short form) in the nav and footer; no multi-step funnels on the homepage.
Treat prints, books, presets, workshops as a secondary 'Shop/Workshops' nav item and include it only if the owner actually sells those things.

Do not rely on testimonials or logo walls; none of the sites read use them on the homepage. Honest trust substitutes: dated news/exhibitions or publications the owner supplies, a short artist statement, and the work itself.
Provide a collapsed 'Open Menu' toggle on mobile and ensure the gallery is a single column or two-up grid that opens a full-size view.
Never render a section that has no content (empty 'Hours', placeholder form messages); omit it.

For client/commission photographers (weddings, portraits), add Portfolio by category, About, Packages/Investment and an enquiry form asking date, location and type of shoot. This comes from vendor guidance in search results, not from a site read; treat as secondary. (derived)

rules.rule: Keep the phone number (click-to-call) and one booking/quote button visible in the header at all times.
Use a sticky call/book bar on mobile so the call is one tap away at any scroll depth.
State the trade, area and what happens next in the first screen, with a primary action built into the hero (ZIP/postcode check or short booking form), not just a brand slogan.
Keep nav to 4-6 items with services grouped under one dropdown; do not list every service in the top bar.
Show services as a tile or card grid with short plain-language labels (drains, repairs, installations, safety checks), 4-10 tiles, each linking to a detail page.
Give 24/7 or emergency availability its own block with phone number and book button, only if the owner really offers it.

Trust order: rating with review count, named review excerpts, written guarantee or pledge, then licensing/insurance; show only ratings and reviews that exist, and never render an empty or broken rating widget (Mr. Electric showed 0/5).

Honest trust substitute when there are no reviews yet: licence/registration number, insurance and guarantee wording the owner supplies, a real photo and name of the tradesperson, a clear pricing policy and the specific area served.
Make the service area explicit (ZIP/postcode lookup or named towns).
Use real photography of technicians, vans and work rather than icons only; keep imagery sparse (one hero photo plus service icons or cards).

rules.rule: Organise the homepage by patient intent: tiles or cards for 'book an appointment', 'find a service/treatment', 'find a location' rather than by internal departments.
Offer a conditions/treatments index grouped by symptom or body system, each linking to a plain-language page.

Use one primary action per screen (book, find a location, call) with the practice phone number and address easy to reach; per-location phone numbers and a location finder where there is more than one site.
Put credentials and regulator links where visitors can verify them (clinician names with registration numbers, regulator rating page); show them only when the owner supplies them.
rules.support: 2 of 2 (different forms: CQC links vs board-certified claim)

rules.rule: Answer cost, insurance and who-it-is-for in a short FAQ near the bottom.

Include a visible 'for emergencies call your local emergency number' notice and a statement of what the practice does not treat; neither homepage carried it prominently (Parsley only in FAQ), so treat this as a safety rule rather than an observed pattern.
Keep hero copy about the patient's need or the care approach, with a calm, light, spacious layout and short sections; avoid urgent, salesy or promo-driven heroes for clinical services.
rules.support: 1 of 2 (Nuffield's promo hero is the counter-example)

rules.rule: Show at most one patient quote, and never use testimonials as evidence of treatment effectiveness.
rules.support: 1 of 2 (Parsley uses one; ASA guidance cited in search says testimonials alone do not substantiate efficacy)

rules.rule: With no reviews or credentials to display yet, use factual practice information the owner supplies: address, opening hours, services, how appointments work, what to bring, fees if known.

Evidence for navigation, imagery, typography and mobile is weak (only two of five sites were readable, one of them partially). The generator should default to a short nav (Services, About/Team, Fees or Insurance, Contact/Book), accessible high-contrast type, and owner-supplied real photography. (derived)

rules.rule: Hero carries one clear action matched to the parent's/learner's intent ('Find a tutor', 'Book a free assessment', 'Find your local centre'), with subjects or levels as quick-pick pills.
Lower the first commitment: free assessment, trial lesson or a ~1-minute form with 'no obligation' wording; show what the first step involves.
Explain the process in 3-4 numbered steps (assess, plan, teach, review).
Make navigation subject/level/age-based (and exam board where relevant) so parents find their child's need in one click.
Show tutor/teacher vetting and child-safeguarding information prominently, using only checks the owner actually performs and can document.
Use a stat band or review count only with a stated basis and date; qualify claims ('on average') and never present unsourced outcome numbers or comparison tables as fact.
rules.support: 3 of 3 use a stat/claim band; 1 of 3 qualifies it, 2 of 3 leave key claims unsourced (the pattern to avoid)

rules.rule: Offer a phone number or enquiry form, with a minimal lead form (parent name, email, phone, postcode, consent).
Disclose limits near the claims (what the free assessment covers, independent tutors, trademarks).
Prefer real photos of the owner's own space and staff; avoid stock child imagery implying real students. Observed sites mostly used stock-style people (2 of 3) or app screenshots.
rules.support: 2 of 3 use stock-style imagery (the pattern to avoid)

rules.rule: With no reviews or results yet: show tutor profiles/qualifications the owner supplies, the lesson format, pricing or 'enquire for pricing', a sample lesson plan and the safeguarding policy.

rules.rule: For listing-led agencies, make the hero a property search (location + price/beds + type); for advisory/boutique agencies, lead instead with a short positioning line and a consultation/valuation action.
Keep the main nav to 3-4 items (Buy, Rent/Sell, About/Offices, Contact) with deeper pages in dropdowns.
Signpost visitor roles with 3-4 cards: buyer, seller, landlord, tenant/renter.
Make 'Book a valuation' or 'Book a consultation' the main seller-side CTA and repeat it after the reviews/proof section.
Provide an office/agent finder and a short enquiry form (name, email, phone, free-text) with consent notice.
Use heritage/scale numbers (years, offices, buyers) and a dated Google rating only from owner-supplied, verifiable data.
Image direction: large, calm photography of homes and interiors with generous white space, only real owner-supplied listing photos for listings; do not use stock photos as if they were listings.
rules.support: 2 of 3 use lifestyle/property imagery; Winkworth's is stock-style

rules.rule: Place regulatory and data notices in the footer (licence/registration statements, equal-opportunity or non-discrimination wording where the market requires it, data-source disclaimers, privacy), shown only as the owner provides them.
Add a lightweight market-insight/articles section if the owner can maintain it; otherwise omit.

With no sales history, awards or reviews: lead with the agent's name, photo, local area knowledge the owner can state specifically, the fee structure and how a valuation works; do not invent figures. (derived)

medical: treatment outcomes, cure rates, success rates, or 'proven/clinically validated' statements
clinician qualifications, specialist status or professional-register numbers (e.g. GMC, NMC, board certification) unless supplied and verifiable
regulator ratings or registrations (e.g. CQC) unless supplied

patient testimonials or star ratings that imply a treatment works (ASA guidance cited in search: testimonials alone are unlikely to substantiate efficacy; the advertiser must hold evidence for objective claims)
claims that could discourage essential medical treatment (CAP Code rule 12.2 as cited)
emergency or 24/7 care, waiting times, same-day appointments
equipment, accreditation or affiliations with hospitals or universities
education: grade improvement figures, pass rates or 'guaranteed results'
'#1', 'top', 'best' or ranking claims without a named basis and date (CAP expects the basis of 'No. 1' claims to be stated)
tutor/teacher qualifications, vetting percentages ('top 5%', '1 in 8'), background-check statements or DBS-type checks unless the owner actually does them and can document
accreditation, inspection ratings or exam-board/school affiliations
student names, photos, scores or testimonials without documented consent
years of operation, number of students/lessons, satisfaction scores
pricing, free-trial terms or guarantee terms
that the owner's tutors are employees, if they are independent contractors
real-estate: sales figures, homes-sold counts, days-on-market, price-achieved percentages

listings, prices or sold prices not supplied by the owner (UK Trading Standards view cited in search: 'price on application' is likely misleading; price, council tax band and tenure are required material information on listings)
licence, registration or redress-scheme membership (e.g. Property Ombudsman, Propertymark) unless supplied
Google or other review ratings and review counts
valuation estimates, market statistics or area price trends
neighbourhood descriptions about schools, crime or demographics (fair-housing and non-discrimination risk in some markets; the search did not verify US rules, so check locally)
stock photography presented as an actual property or team
